newsitem.title: USA: G7 summit split on environmental issues.
newsitem.headline: G7 summit split on environmental issues.

text.p: A largely scripted summit of the world's leading industrial nations stumbled on environmental issues on Saturday but issued an upbeat bulletin on the global economy and warned Balkan leaders they would suffer if Bosnia's peace collapsed.
Leaders of the Group of Seven nations and Russia, meeting in this Rocky Mountain city for an annual summit, split on how much to cut gases blamed for global warming and climate changes.

In a rare moment of dissent in the carefully orchestrated and low-key summit, Britain, France, Germany and Italy attacked U.S reluctance to agree to a cut of 15 percent in carbon dioxide and other emissions by the year 2010.
The split could spill over into next week's U.N.-sponsored Earth Summit II in New York.
"There is a real divergence of views between, on one hand the Europeans and on the other the Americans -- not Canada, the United States," French President Jacques Chirac said.

The summit partners papered over differences on plans to pull American peacekeepers out of Bosnia by mid-1998 and concentrated on telling the former warring parties that aid could be stopped if they let the peace process falter.
They singled out Croatia and Serbia for special criticism, faulting them for lack of commitment to the peace process.

The summit nations - the United States, Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Canada and Russia -- said in a draft communique they expected China to uphold its commitment to preserving civil liberties in Hong Kong when Beijing regains control of the British colony on July 1.
Officials said the communique also "looked forward" to China holding democratic elections for a new legislature in Hong Kong as soon as possible after the handover.

Gathered at a round table at the Denver Public Library, the world leaders were urged by Clinton to "pool our strength" and confront common problems. Before they could do that they had to solve an immediate crisis -- finding a chair for British Prime Minister Tony Blair.
Clinton gave Russian President Boris Yeltsin pride of place, seating him at his right hand for a session on post-Cold War dilemmas. But he was barred from attending the global economy discussion.
The G7 countries welcomed signs of an improving world economy but said more needed to be done to ensure that the good times continued, according to statement issued later.
They also set out specific goals for their countries to help ensure that global expansion remains on track.
"We have been encouraged by the many positive indicators in our economies," they said. "But we still have work to do."
Among the encouraging signs: low inflation, reduced budget deficits and solid growth. But unemployment remains high in some countries, particularly among the young.

Clinton and Blair, at a private meeting on the sidelines, both agreed that Northern Ireland peace talks could not include Sinn Fein, the political arm of the outlawed Irish Republican Army, unless the IRA agreed to a ceasefire.
Blair told Clinton that Britain had previously promised Sinn Fein it could have a seat at peace talks if the IRA observed a written six-week ceasefire, British officials said.
But they said the IRA response to the dramatic initiative was to murder two policemen in an ambush in Lurgan, southwest of Belfast, on Monday.

While the presidents and prime ministers spoke, Hillary Rodham Clinton took the leaders' wives by train to a 10,700-foot (3,300-metre) mountain in the Rockies for a lunch and exhibition of square dancing.
On the lighter side, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl led a revolt against President Bill Clinton's plans to have the leaders wear cowboy boots to a "Saturday Night at the Summit" variety musical show.

"We had a long discussion about boots and Kohl said that he would never wear them, absolutely never," said Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi. He said Clinton and Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien agreed to wear boots on behalf of all.

The summit leaders wrapped up their day of serious discussions about Africa, terrorism and the world economy with a 19th century "cookout" at a restaurant in nearby Morrison, where the menu featured buffalo and rattlesnake.
